note: Eight small Noir programs, each recorded by `nargo trace` into the container beside its sources. The corpus has three consumers and one reason to stay correct: it is what BlockTracer's `demo` chain publishes, it is a fixture the shared CodeTracer ViewModels can be driven from, and it is what desktop CodeTracer can open. Regenerate with `fixtures/trace/tour/record.sh`.
caveats: `nargo trace` is not byte-deterministic: `meta.dat` carries a UUIDv7 recording id minted at close, and the embedded workdir string. Everything else — every step, call and value — is identical between runs. The containers are therefore VENDORED, never regenerated at build time, because the demo tree must be byte-identical for a given seed and CI generates it twice and diffs.

The pinned recorder predates noir@6939457ff7 (`embed the compiled source text in the .ct container`), so every container here reports `source_views: []`. Source text reaches a reader through the `sources/` tree beside each container, which the demo generator publishes as a source bundle. Re-recording with a newer tracer would embed the sources and change the pin; do that deliberately.
`nargo trace` compiles with `force_brillig`, so every program is executed unconstrained regardless of how it is written. That is a property of the recorder, not of the programs.

Three things the tracer cannot record and which therefore appear in no program here: `enum` values (the value marshaller reaches an unimplemented case and aborts the recording), user-defined `#[oracle(...)]` calls (`nargo trace` exposes no resolver, and an oracle body is never instrumented), and `Field` values above 2^63 (a recorded `Field` is truncated to `i64`, so every program keeps its field values small).

capabilities.title: The loop rail and per-iteration navigation
An execution that stops on a constraint

programs.title: Types and values
programs.summary: Every value kind the language has, brought into scope one line at a time. The subject is the Values pane: a reader stepping through should be able to name the type of every row they see.
expectations: `weights[0] + weights[2]` is 3 + 4, so `from_array` is 7 — and the program asserts it, so a recording in which it is not 7 did not finish.
`flag` is `small > 100` with `small = 200`, so it is true; `from_tuple` is the same value read back out of a tuple.
`body.position` is a struct nested inside a struct, so the Values pane must render a compound whose field is itself compound.
`trail` is a vector of length 3 built by two `push_back` calls on a one-element vector, so its recorded length changes while the binding does not.

`negative` is `-42` and `signed_wide` is `-100_000`. The recorder writes signed integers as their two's-complement unsigned value, so these read 214 and 4294867296 — a fidelity gap in value rendering, demonstrated here rather than described.

programs.title: Loops and iteration
programs.summary: Three loop shapes, chosen so the loop rail has iterations worth moving between and values that differ from one iteration to the next. A loop whose variables never change is a rail with nothing on it.
expectations: `triangular(6)` sums 0..5, so `acc` takes the sequence 0, 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 across the loop's rungs and returns 15.
`grid_sum(3, 4)` has an outer rail of 3 rungs, each containing an inner rail of 4; `row_total` resets at the top of every outer iteration and the total is 0+1+...+11 = 66.
`collatz_steps(27)` runs 111 iterations. The count is not readable off the source — which is the point of recording it.
`first_gap(30)` skips every even candidate via `continue` and ends via `break` on the first odd composite, 9.
`sieve::is_prime` is in a second file, so stepping into it crosses a document boundary.

programs.title: Branches and conditions
programs.summary: Every `if` here is written so that both arms are reachable and the inputs decide, and each classifier is called more than once with values landing in different arms — so the same source line is marked taken on one visit and not-taken on another.
expectations: `classify` has three arms and is reached once, from `describe`'s middle arm, with `value = 12` — so it returns 1 and its other two arms are evaluated-and-not-taken on that visit.

`describe` is called three times: sensor 1 with -77 (known and extreme, so 9), sensor 2 with 12 (known, not extreme, so `classify` runs), sensor 7 (unknown, so 255). All three of its arms run across the recording, and each runs on exactly one visit.

`clamp` is called three times with `(lo, hi) = (-10, 10)`: -77 takes the low arm, 3 takes neither, 88 takes the high arm. The middle call reaches the outer `else` and then does NOT take the inner `if` — an arm that was evaluated and declined, which is a different fact from an arm that was never reached.
The three clamp results are asserted, so a recording that reaches the end had them right.

programs.title: Calls and recursion
programs.summary: A call tree worth looking at rather than a flat list: direct recursion several frames deep, two functions calling each other, tree recursion that branches, and a helper reached from two different parents.
expectations: `factorial(5)` puts six frames of one function on the stack, each with a different `n`, and returns 120 — which the program asserts.
`is_even(4)` alternates `is_even`/`is_odd` down to zero, so the trace shows two names interleaving over five frames.
`fib(6)` branches rather than descending, and returns 8 — asserted.

`arith::mix` has two distinct parents in the tree: `checksum`, which calls it four times, and `main`, which calls it once directly. A call trace aggregated by function must show five frames of it; one ordered by call must show them under two parents.
`arith::rotate` is the deepest frame and the only one in that module with a loop, so a step-out from it returns into a loop iteration.

programs.title: Generics and traits
programs.summary: Source written once and executed several times over different types. A generic function has one body and many instantiations; a trait method has one name and many bodies. Both make "which code is running" a real question, and the call trace is where it is answered.
expectations: `largest` has one body and three instantiations in this recording — `u32`, `u64` and `i32` — so the call trace names the same function three times over three types.
`sum_all` is a numeric generic instantiated at N=3 and N=5, so the same source line is a loop of three rungs on one visit and five on another. `sum_all([1,2,3])` is 6, which the program asserts.
`Circle` does not override `Shape::perimeter` and `Rect` does, so the same call spelling in `describe` reaches the default body on one visit and the impl's own on the other.
`Circle { radius: 3 }` has area 3*3*3 = 27 and perimeter 27*2 = 54 by the default method; `Rect { w: 6, h: 7 }` has area 42 and perimeter 26.
`Field` deliberately has no `Ord` impl, which is why `largest` is never instantiated at `Field` — a language fact the source states in a comment rather than leaving to a compiler error.

programs.title: Program output and the event log
programs.summary: The stream of things the execution SAID, as distinct from the values it held. In this language that stream is `print`, `println` and format strings, and it is the only pane whose content a program author writes directly.
expectations: The first entry is the bare string `=== invoice ===` and the last is `=== end ===`, so the log has a readable beginning and end rather than being a repeated sentence.
The loop runs 4 times and writes two entries per iteration — one from `line_total`, one frame deeper, and one from `main` — so log entries and loop rungs line up.
Line i has qty i+2 and unit price 10+i, so the four line totals are 2*10=20, 3*11=33, 4*12=48 and 5*13=65, and the subtotal is 166.
166 is below the threshold of 300, so `apply_discount` takes its `else` arm and the log says `no discount: 166 is below 300`.
`print("subtotal: ")` without a newline and the `println` after it are two separate events that a reader sees as one sentence — the log's entries are writes, not lines.
A format string interpolates bindings and not field accesses, so every value printed here is bound to a local first. Those locals exist only to be printed, and are what the log's text is built from.

programs.title: Constraints, and an execution that fails one
programs.summary: What a recording looks like when the program does NOT finish. This is the case a zero-knowledge debugger exists for: a constraint did not hold, and the question is which one, on which values, reached from where. The recording ends at the failing assertion.
expectations: Four assertions in `transfer` are evaluated and hold, twice each, before any assertion fails — so one recording contains both `checked and passed` and `checked and stopped`.

Alice opens at 120 and Bob at 50. After transferring 30 to Bob they are 90 and 80; after Bob transfers 10 back they are 100 and 70. The total is 170 throughout, which is what the conservation assertion checks.
`solvency_margin(alice, bob, 1_000_000)` compares 170 against a floor of a million, so it returns 0.
The recording therefore STOPS at `assert(margin > 0, ...)`. The last entry in its event log is the message `accounts must clear the reserve floor`, and there is no step after it.
The failure is unsatisfiable by construction, not by accident — a reader stepping into `solvency_margin` can see the two balances and the floor side by side and work out why the next line stops.

programs.title: Bounds, limits and overflow
programs.summary: What happens at the EDGES of a type. In a circuit this is not a curiosity: an addition that overflows is a failed constraint, and the difference between wrapping and aborting is the difference between a proof and no proof.
expectations: `saturating_add(u32::MAX - 2, 10)` detects that the addition would pass the ceiling and returns `u32::max_value()` = 4294967295, which the program asserts. Nothing overflows, which is the point: the check is in the source rather than in the failure.

`wrapping_walk(203)` adds `u32::MAX / 2` three times with `wrapping_add`, so the value passes the ceiling twice and lands on 2147483848 — modular arithmetic asked for explicitly rather than arrived at by accident.
`shift_ladder` applies all ten compound-assignment operators and both shifts in order, so the recording holds ten successive values of one binding and the result is 274.

`first_over(500)` is a `loop` whose trip count appears in no bound in the source: it multiplies by 3 from 1 and breaks at 729, the sixth iteration. It returns `Option::some(729)`, which the Values pane renders as a struct with a boolean tag.
`bounds` is SHADOWED — the second `let bounds` is a new binding, and the first is still in the recording at the steps before it. `Bounds::new(0, 8)` widened by 500 has span 508 and midpoint 254.
`span()` takes `&self` and returns the same 508 as the destructured arithmetic, which `assert_eq` checks. Reading through a reference is recorded correctly; only WRITING through one is not (NR-04).
`window` is declared `[u32; Window::<3>]` where `Window<let N: u32>: u32 = N * 2`, so the compiler computes its length as 6 and `window.len() == 6` holds.

programs.title: Mutation over time
programs.summary: A value that CHANGES. Everything else in this tour shows values computed and bound once; this one shows the same binding holding a different value at a different time, which is the case a time-travelling debugger answers and a printout of the final state does not. The forms the recorder captures come first; the one it does not is last, alone and labelled.
expectations: `ramp(5, 7)` rebinds `level` three times, so the recording holds its whole history — 5, 12, 24, 23 — and stepping backward walks it in reverse. The result 23 is asserted.

`accumulate([1,2,3,4,5])` adds each value and subtracts one per iteration, so `total` is recorded at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 11 across the loop and returns 10 — asserted. Compound assignment inside a loop is a statement kind this tracer has previously failed to instrument, leaving the variable frozen while the circuit computed the right answer; the full sequence being present is the check.

`tally(4)` assigns into a compound by FIELD and by INDEX — three distinct assignment targets. `a` is recorded at {0,0}, {0,1}, {1,1}, {1,2}, {3,2}, {3,3}, {6,3}, {6,4}; `arr` becomes [0,6,0] then [0,6,4]; the result is 10, which `assert_eq` checks. These forms are in the corpus because `tools/noir-coverage.mjs` enumerates the compiler's `LValue` variants and reported them as neither demonstrated nor explained — not because anybody remembered them.

`run_counter(5)` records six successive `Counter` structs — {5,0}, {6,1}, {7,2}, {8,3}, {0,3}, {1,4} — so the Values pane shows one binding whose nested field moves. The fifth is `reset_if_above(7)` taking its reset arm because 8 > 7, which is also what the branch marking should say.
The recording contains no error event: every assertion in this program holds, including the one about the writes the recording does not show.

`bump(&mut slot, step)` is called three times, so the recording should show `slot` taking 5, 12, 19 and 26 in `main`, and `*slot` should have a value inside `bump`. IT DOES NOT — see this program's `knownFailures`. The expectation is written as what SHOULD happen, because a corpus that asserted the broken behaviour would teach the next reader that absence is correct and would go red the day somebody fixed it.

knownFailures.expectation: The recording shows `slot` at 5, 12, 19 and 26 in `main`, and a dereferenced value for `*slot` inside `bump`.
knownFailures.reason: Writes through a `&mut` parameter are not captured. Noir's own debug instrumenter emits a literal `0` in place of the assignment oracle for `*x = ...` (noirc_frontend/src/debug/mod.rs:425, present verbatim upstream); the stub it would have called is named `__debug_dereference_assign` while the debugger dispatches on `__debug_deref_assign`, so the two halves could never meet; and the handler is `unimplemented!()` anyway. The caller's binding is never re-recorded after the call, and `PrintableType::Reference` decodes to `Other`, which our tracer renders as `ValueRecord::None`.
knownFailures.evidence: fixtures/trace/tour/mutation/tour_mutation.ct at recorder 906af2f42d: `slot` is recorded once, as 5, and never again; inside `bump` it reads `{"kind":"None"}`. The program's own `assert(slot == start + 3 * step)` HOLDS, so the circuit performed all three writes the recording does not show.
knownFailures.closed_by: An upstream change to noir-lang/noir. It needs all four of: instrumenter emission for `LValue::Dereference`, reconciling `__debug_dereference_assign` with `__debug_deref_assign`, a real `DebugVars::assign_deref`, and a `PrintableValue` that carries reference contents. See docs/NOIR-RECORDER-DEFECTS.md NR-04. UNOWNED.

check.note: Holds while `slot` never reaches 26. When it does, the write through the reference is being recorded, the defect is fixed, and check-corpus.sh fails demanding this entry be removed.

sets.recordable: `programs` — each produces a recording BlockTracer publishes and serves. These are the capability tour, and they are the set the E2E layer selects.
sets.toolchain: `toolchainPrograms` — each exercises the Noir toolchain and CANNOT produce a servable recording: it fails to compile, or the recorder cannot represent it. Still tests, and still the reason the tour is written the way it is; checked by `check-corpus.sh`.

toolchainPrograms.title: Enums and `match`
toolchainPrograms.why: Correct Noir that executes correctly and cannot be recorded. `nargo execute -Zenums` prints the right answer; `nargo trace -Zenums` panics in OUR tracer's value marshaller. It is also the reason no tour program uses an enum.

expect.match: Tracing support for enums is not yet implemented
expect.shouldBe: `nargo trace -Zenums` records the program, and an enum value renders as ValueRecord::Variant.

toolchainPrograms.title: An oracle call
toolchainPrograms.why: An oracle is how an unconstrained function asks the outside world for a value it then constrains — a headline language feature the tour cannot show. `nargo execute` has --oracle-resolver and --oracle-file; `nargo trace` has neither.

expect.shouldBe: `nargo trace` takes the same oracle-resolution flags as `nargo execute`, so an oracle program can be recorded faithfully.

toolchainPrograms.title: `Field` has no ordering
toolchainPrograms.why: A language rule, not a defect: a field element wraps, so `>` is not a question it answers. This is why tour/generics instantiates `largest` over u32, u64 and i32 and never over Field.

expect.match: No matching impl found for `Field: Ord`

toolchainPrograms.title: A signed integer cannot be cast straight to `Field`
toolchainPrograms.why: A language rule. A negative signed value has no field representation that agrees with arithmetic, so the language refuses rather than picking a convention silently. tour/values routes signed values through an unsigned width.

expect.match: Only unsigned integer types may be casted to Field

toolchainPrograms.title: A format string interpolates bindings, not expressions
toolchainPrograms.why: A language rule that shapes two tour programs more than any other: every value tour/events and tour/constraints print is bound to a local first, and a reader who did not know this rule would take those locals for clutter.

expect.match: Field access isn't supported in format strings
